approachQuestion.prompt:
Rolling load ledger. Consume n signed integer values from a forward-only stream. After each value arrives, compute the sum of the last k values seen, or all seen values if fewer than k have arrived. Add that sum to a checksum and return the final checksum. n and k are given in advance; 1 <= k <= n <= 200,000. Values, rolling sums, and checksum fit signed 64-bit. The stream cannot be revisited or inspected ahead. Indexed storage, word addition/subtraction and modulo arithmetic cost constant time. Minimize worst-case total time, then peak auxiliary space. Only the final checksum is output.

Example 1: Input: values=[3,-1,4,2], k=2. Output: 14; successive sums are 3,2,3,6.
Example 2: Input: values=[5,-2], k=1. Output: 3.

options.text: Use a k-slot circular buffer and a running sum. When replacing a full slot, subtract its old value before adding and storing the new value; add the running sum to the checksum each step.
options.feedback: A value is needed only until it leaves the recent k positions. The circular buffer retains exactly that bounded history while the running sum avoids rescanning it.

options.text: Append every seen value to a growing array, maintain a running sum, and subtract the array entry k positions back when one exists.
options.feedback: The sums are correct and avoid repeated scans, but the complete history remains stored even after older values can never affect another sum.

options.text: Store all values seen so far and recompute each rolling sum by scanning the most recent up to k entries.
options.feedback: This computes the correct checksum, but after warm-up it repeats a full recent-range scan for every new arrival. Maintaining the rolling sum removes those repeated additions.

options.text: Add every arrival to one running sum and add that sum to the checksum without removing old values.
options.feedback: For [5,-2], k=1, this adds 5 then 3 for checksum 8; the required rolling sums are 5 and -2, giving 3.

feedback.reason: Live history is determined by how long a value can affect future answers, not by the total number of arrivals.
details: Allocate and zero k slots. Keep a write index, count of values seen capped at k, rolling sum and checksum. On arrival, if the buffer is full subtract the current slot; store and add the new value, advance the index modulo k, and add the updated rolling sum to checksum. Return only checksum.

With k=2 and arrivals 4,7,3, rolling totals are 4,11,10. Before overwriting 4's slot, subtract 4 from the live sum, then add 3. The stream cannot be revisited, so the ring stores values needed for future expiration rather than merely caching redundant input.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze circular-recent-values for n arrivals and window length k, with k<=n. Include allocating/zeroing the k slots and every update. No stream history is retained outside the circular buffer. Input and final checksum are excluded; there is no recursion or hashing.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

options.text: O(n + k) time, O(k) auxiliary space
O(n + k) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + k) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Initialize k slots and do fixed work per arrival; those slots are auxiliary.
details: Initialization costs O(k). Every arrival then performs constant work, yielding O(n+k), equivalently O(n) under k<=n. The k slots remain live and count as auxiliary; counters and sums add constant storage. Older values are overwritten only once their contributions have been subtracted.
“O(nk) time, O(k) auxiliary space”: The running sum removes the need to traverse k retained values after each arrival.
“O(n + k) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This is a loose storage bound when k is much smaller than n; the method retains only k values.
“O(n + k) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The outgoing value is required for subtraction, and the analyzed method stores k such values in its buffer.
